\begin{abstract}
When a model improves at a structured task after seeing earlier examples in context, has it abstracted the structure or reused the examples? Behavioural improvement alone cannot tell: longer contexts, recall and exemplar matching all produce it. We introduce a compounding fingerprint for in-context completion of partial Cayley tables written in fresh word labels. Each queried cell is labelled by the weakest axiom class that forces it (Latin, loop or associativity), and each history of earlier complete tables is controlled by a length-matched scramble, held-out isomorphism types, a recall (leak) control and non-associative loops. A preregistered decision rule recovers seven exact idealised learners without error; only held-out transfer cleanly separates abstraction from exemplar matching. Nine checkpoints (ten model--precision configurations) from three families, up to 8B, are all recall-only. None infers Latin-forced cells in direct-answer mode, and none compounds ($t = 4$ minus scramble: $-$0.019 to +0.026, every CI including 0), although Qwen3 at 4--8B recalls seen tables at 0.95--0.96. Small from-scratch transformers instead learn a global count shortcut, which a post-hoc count learner matches to within 0.001--0.007 in five of six learned networks. The released In-Context Algebra model, our positive control, is classified above recall but not as Bayes-type: at $t = 0$, Latin- and loop-forced cells score 0.89--0.99, associativity-forced cells 0.53--0.70. The activation-space compute--retrieve axis from our earlier preprint moves significantly in the predicted direction in none of five models on a format- and length-matched retrieval/inference contrast and is significantly reversed in three; context vocabulary explains 64--87\% of the reversal (exploratory).
\end{abstract}
\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}

A learner compounds experience when solving earlier problems makes later, related problems cheaper to solve. Learning to learn has a natural in-context form in language models: if a prompt holds several complete instances of a structured task, the model may do better on the next instance than it would without them. Such improvement is often read as evidence that the model has abstracted the shared structure. The reading matters, because an abstraction transfers to instances that share the structure but none of the surface, whereas reuse of the examples does not.

Behavioural improvement alone cannot establish abstraction, because at least three other explanations produce it. First, every added example lengthens the context, and context length by itself changes performance. Second, if an earlier example contains the answer, a model can recall or copy it without any inference. Third, a model can match the new instance against the stored examples and answer by analogy to the closest one. Exemplar matching improves with more examples just as abstraction does, and the two differ only on types that the history does not contain. In information-theoretic terms, a learner that stores the examples verbatim and one that has extracted their rules hold the same information about the task; they differ only in what that information makes cheaply usable~\cite{xu2020usable}. A test of compounding therefore has to control context length, separate recall from inference, and include held-out types.

Algebraic operation tables make such a test exact. A partial Cayley table, with some cells revealed and the rest queried, determines some of its missing cells under weak assumptions and others only under strong ones. Whether a queried cell is fixed by the Latin property alone, by the loop axioms (identity and cancellation), or only through associativity can be decided exactly, by enumeration or SAT, for every cell of every trial. Each cell thus receives a \emph{forcing class}, which states what a learner must know to answer it. Writing each table in fresh, arbitrary word labels removes semantic cues, and the earlier tables can be manipulated directly: replaced by length-matched tables without group structure, restricted to isomorphism types other than the target's, or made to contain the target's own labelled table. Exact idealised learners can then be run on the very trials the models see.

The closest work is In-Context Algebra~\cite{todd2026ica}. Todd et al. train small transformers on sequences of group facts, with symbols reassigned in every sequence, and identify the networks' mechanisms: commutative copying, identity recognition and closure-based cancellation, with associative composition the weakest route. They do not measure how accuracy depends on the number of earlier tables, label cells by forcing class, compare against an exemplar baseline at equal budget, or evaluate pretrained language models. A second line of work asks whether in-context learners memorise or generalise. Ravent\'os et al.~\cite{raventos2023} find a task-diversity threshold below which a transformer behaves like a Bayesian predictor over the discrete set of its pretraining tasks, and Wurgaft et al.~\cite{wurgaft2025} cast the trade-off between such memorising and generalising predictors in a hierarchical Bayesian account. Our exemplar and abstraction learners are in-context analogues of these two predictors, with the ``seen tasks'' supplied in the prompt under fresh labels rather than in pretraining. Chan et al.~\cite{chan2022} report that transformers generalise from context mainly through exemplars and from weights mainly through rules, while pretrained language models generalise from context in a more rule-based way; held-out types test this contrast directly. Under the view of in-context learning as implicit Bayesian inference~\cite{xie2021}, a learner that already holds the true environment prior gains nothing from earlier tables written in fresh labels, and our Bayesian baselines make that prediction exact. Matsutani et al.~\cite{matsutani2026} report gains from relabelled demonstrations of other worlds in Qwen3 base models, but with one shared vocabulary and, as far as we found, no length-matched control. We know of no published evaluation of pretrained language models on in-context group-table completion with fresh labels.

We turn this design into a \emph{compounding fingerprint}. A model sees a \textbf{history} of $t = 0$, 1, 2 or 4 complete earlier tables, each written in its own fresh single-token English words, followed by a target table of order $n = 5$, 6 or 8 (a group, or in one $n = 5$ cell a loop) that reveals $k$ of its cells, the \textbf{cue}. Every unrevealed cell is queried and scored by forced choice, and every cell carries its forcing class: Latin-forced (L), loop-forced (O), associativity-forced (G), forced only by commutativity or cyclicity (Ab, Cy), or undetermined (U). Base histories are compared with a length-matched \textbf{scramble control}, \textbf{held-out types}, a \textbf{leak control} that contains the target's own labelled table, and non-associative loops, over 1,800 trials per model. A preregistered decision rule maps the resulting signature to the learner classes R, N, N\_iso, A and B-type. We applied it to seven exact idealised learners, to nine checkpoints (ten model--precision configurations) from three families~\cite{qwen3,smollm2,olmo2}, to seven small transformers trained from scratch, and to the released In-Context Algebra model. We used the same stimuli to test an activation-space direction from our own earlier preprint, the compute--retrieve (CR) axis~\cite{ramdan2026cr}. The three largest pretrained models ran in 4-bit nf4 quantisation, whose preregistered control failed its tolerance. All model inference and training ran on one 8 GB laptop GPU, and every deviation from preregistration is listed in Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}.

Our contributions are:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{An exact, preregistered measurement.} On identical trials, the decision rule returns the correct class for all seven idealised learners at $n = 6$ and $n = 8$, with 0 misclassifications. At $n = 6$, abstraction and exemplar matching both gain about +0.70 over scramble on G cells, and only held-out transfer separates them cleanly: +0.70 for abstraction against +0.03 for exemplar matching (Section~\ref{sec:r-ideal}).
  \item \textbf{A calibrated null for pretrained models up to 8B.} All ten configurations are class R. None compounds: four history tables minus the length-matched scramble lies between $-$0.019 and +0.026, and every 95\% CI includes 0. None infers Latin-forced cells in direct-answer mode; in the eight models swept over cue density, this holds even at dense cues where one-pass row/column elimination would score 0.92 (post hoc). Recall is family-dependent: Qwen3 recalls a previously seen labelled table at 0.95--0.96 at 4--8B, OLMo-2 at 0.31--0.37 (Section~\ref{sec:r-llm}; Section~\ref{sec:r-cal}).
  \item \textbf{A count baseline.} Small transformers trained from scratch on group, Latin and loop diets learn a global count shortcut: they answer with the symbol least represented in the cue. The post-hoc count learner C matches five of the six learned networks to within 0.001--0.007. On the in-training evaluation the shortcut alone scores 0.33 at $n = 6$, enough to pass the preregistered learning-failure threshold (Section~\ref{sec:r-trained}).
  \item \textbf{A positive control on a real network.} The released In-Context Algebra model is classified non-R, non-B: at $t = 0$, Latin- and loop-forced cells score 0.89--0.99 and associativity-forced cells 0.53--0.70. In a post hoc split, it beats an exact loop-level baseline at $n = 6$ and $n = 8$ but not at $n = 5$, and it partly answers by commutative copying. Its class changes during training (exploratory). Its 16-token vocabulary leaves the compounding branch untested (Section~\ref{sec:r-ica}).
  \item \textbf{A validity test for activation ``mode'' probes.} The CR axis separates its own calibration prompts with AUC 0.96--0.99, but on a format- and length-matched retrieval/inference contrast it moves significantly in the predicted direction (CI excluding 0) in 0 of 5 models and is significantly reversed in 3. In an exploratory control, context vocabulary explains 64--87\% of the reversal; with vocabulary matched, a retrieval signal of the predicted sign appears in the post-trained model and without the chat template (Section~\ref{sec:r-cr}).
\end{itemize}

Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work. Section~\ref{sec:fingerprint} defines the task, the forcing classes, the history conditions, the idealised learners and the decision rule. Section~\ref{sec:setup} describes the models, calibration, trained networks, reasoning probe, CR-axis test, positive control and statistics. Section~\ref{sec:results} reports the results, Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses what they do and do not establish, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} states the open problems.

\section{Related work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{In-context learning of algebraic structure}

The closest prior work is \emph{In-Context Algebra}~\cite{todd2026ica}. Todd et al. train small transformers (4 layers, 8 heads, width 1024) on sequences of facts $xy = z$ from cyclic groups C3--C10 and dihedral groups D3--D5 (as the paper states; the released code for the checkpoint we score also samples D2 = Z2$\times$Z2), with the map from group elements to tokens redrawn for every sequence. Their models reach near-perfect accuracy, transfer to held-out order-8 groups, and use identifiable mechanisms: commutative copying, identity recognition and closure-based cancellation. Associative composition is the weakest route, at 60.2\% on the sequences that test it. Our forcing classes (Section~\ref{sec:classes}) make this an exact per-cell measurement: a loop-forced (O) cell is fixed by identity and cancellation alone, an associativity-forced (G) cell only through associativity. Scored this way, the released In-Context Algebra model is the first real network for which the fingerprint returns a class above R, with Latin- and loop-forced cells at 0.89--0.99 and G cells at 0.53--0.70 at $t = 0$, in line with the authors' ranking of mechanisms (Section~\ref{sec:r-ica}). That work evaluates no pretrained language models and does not measure how completion depends on the number of earlier, differently labelled tables; the released model's 16-token vocabulary fits at most one history table, so our compounding contrast cannot be measured on it. Adjacent work studies algebra learned in weights: grokking of finite-dimensional algebras~\cite{notsawo2026grokking}, and in-context modular arithmetic that generalises out of distribution only above a threshold number of pretraining tasks~\cite{he2024grok}. ``Cayley-table completion'' in~\cite{huh2025algebraic,huh2026cayley} is a different problem, recovering a table by tensor factorisation rather than inferring it in context.

\paragraph{Memorising and generalising learners}

Ravent\'os et al.~\cite{raventos2023} find a task-diversity threshold in transformers trained on linear regression: below it the model acts as a Bayesian estimator over the discrete set of pretraining tasks, above it as ridge regression. Wurgaft et al.~\cite{wurgaft2025} explain such transitions as a posterior-weighted trade-off between a memorising and a generalising predictor. Our exemplar learner N\_iso and abstraction learner A (Section~\ref{sec:learners}) are in-context analogues of these predictors, with the ``seen tasks'' supplied in the prompt under fresh labels. On identical trials both gain about +0.70 over the scramble control on G cells, and only held-out types separate them cleanly: +0.70 for A against +0.03 for N\_iso (Section~\ref{sec:r-ideal}). Chan et al.~\cite{chan2022} report that transformers trained on controlled stimuli generalise from context mainly through exemplars, whereas pretrained language models do so in a more rule-based way, increasingly with scale. Our design would also separate the two by the shape of compounding (gradual for exemplar matching, a step at $t = 1$ for abstraction), but none of the nine pretrained checkpoints compounds, so the prediction remains untested. If in-context learning is implicit Bayesian inference~\cite{xie2021}, a learner that already holds the true environment prior gains nothing from fresh-label histories; our Bayes learner B makes this exact, scoring 1.000 on G cells with and without a history.

\paragraph{Recall and induction-style copying}

Mechanistic work traces in-context learning to identifiable circuits. Induction heads complete a repeated pattern AB\ldots{}A with B and coincide with a phase change in in-context ability~\cite{olsson2022}, and symbol-abstraction, symbolic-induction and retrieval heads together carry out abstract rule induction in language models~\cite{yang2025symbolic}. Our recall-only learner R corresponds to verbatim, induction-style copying, and the leak control, whose last history table is the target's own labelled table, measures that ability directly. Recall depends on family more than on size: under the leak control, G-cell accuracy is 0.52--0.65 for Qwen3 models up to 1.7B, 0.95 and 0.96 for Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, 0.44 for SmolLM2-1.7B and 0.31--0.37 for OLMo-2, yet every one of these models is class R (Section~\ref{sec:r-llm}). In the larger Qwen3 models, then, the absence of compounding is not a failure to read the context; the prerequisite inference is missing.

\paragraph{Pretrained models and structure defined in context}

Several studies ask whether pretrained models adopt semantics defined only in the prompt. Overriding flipped labels and learning from semantically unrelated labels emerge with scale~\cite{wei2023larger}. Performance on counterfactual task variants, such as arithmetic in unfamiliar bases, degrades relative to the default task~\cite{wu2024reasoning}, and language models underperform simple n-gram baselines on randomly sampled formal languages~\cite{gupta2025random}. Analyses across the Pythia suite place in-context learning between memorisation and an independent symbolic algorithm~\cite{niu2025illusion}. Models reorganise their representations to match a graph defined only by random walks in context~\cite{park2024iclr}, yet often cannot use such representations downstream~\cite{lepori2026}, and representational change within a context suggests that in-context learning is not one process~\cite{hosseini2026}. Our null result fits this picture: up to 8B, no checkpoint infers Latin-forced cells in direct-answer mode, and none of the eight swept over cue density does so even at the densest cue, where one-pass row/column elimination would score 0.92 (post hoc; Section~\ref{sec:r-cal}).

\paragraph{Cross-episode gains and length-matched controls}

Matsutani et al.~\cite{matsutani2026} come closest to compounding: few-shot demonstrations from different worlds, with the same or a different graph topology, improve in-context world modelling across several model families. Their worlds reassign one shared set of words to the graph's nodes, whereas our history tables use fresh words, and we found no length-matched control like our scramble history. Two raw increases from $t = 0$ to $t = 4$ in our data were reliable, and both vanish against the scramble history; for OLMo-2-1B at $n = 6$, t4 $-$ t0 is +0.042 [+0.011, +0.073], but t4 $-$ scramble is +0.020 [$-$0.008, +0.051]. Across all ten model--precision configurations, t4 $-$ scramble lies between $-$0.019 and +0.026, with every 95\% CI including 0 (Section~\ref{sec:r-llm}).

\paragraph{Activation-space probes of processing mode}

A separate line reads the processing mode from activations. Demonstrations are compressed into a task vector~\cite{hendel2023} or a function vector carried by a few attention heads~\cite{todd2023fv}, and the Jacobian lens identifies representations a model is poised to verbalise, which carry intermediate steps of silent reasoning while automatic processing proceeds without them, as in a global workspace~\cite{gurnee2026workspace}. The compute--retrieve (CR) axis~\cite{ramdan2026cr} probes mode directly: a mean-difference direction from 30 retrieval and 30 computation prompts, where ``retrieve'' means recall of facts stored in weights. That preprint notes that its retrieval prompts are shorter than the computation prompts, leaving prompt complexity as a possible confound. Our leak and base conditions remove it for in-context retrieval: they share format, token count and query position, yet accuracy is 0.53--0.97 in leak and 0.17--0.22 in base. The axis separates its own calibration prompts with AUC 0.96--0.99, but on this contrast it moves significantly in the predicted direction in 0 of 5 Qwen3 models and is significantly reversed in 3 (Section~\ref{sec:r-cr}). In an exploratory control, context vocabulary explains 64--87\% of the reversal; with vocabulary matched, a retrieval signal of the predicted sign appears in the post-trained model ($d_{z}$ +0.36) and without the chat template ($d_{z}$ +0.33 to +1.67). Whether such representations would carry induced axioms across tables is untested.

\paragraph{Usable information and critical sets}

Storing past tables verbatim and extracting their axioms yield the same Shannon information about the environment. Predictive V-information~\cite{xu2020usable} instead measures what a computationally bounded observer can use, and computation can create it. This frames our equal-budget comparison: N\_iso and A enumerate at most the same number of candidate tables and differ only in what the history makes cheaply usable. For Latin squares, a critical set is a minimal set of entries that determines the square, and the smallest one corresponds to the minimum teaching dimension of the class~\cite{hatami2016}. Our forcing classes ask a cell-level version for one fixed cue: which unrevealed cells it already determines, and under which of the nested classes Latin, loop and group.

\section{The compounding fingerprint}\label{sec:fingerprint}

The compounding fingerprint has four parts: a table-completion task in which earlier tables can be shown or withheld, an exact label for every queried cell, history conditions that isolate what the history contributes, and a preregistered decision rule that maps the resulting signature to a learner class.

\subsection{Task}\label{sec:task}

A trial presents one or more operation tables as facts \texttt{x * y = z}, one per line in random order, over words that are single tokens. Each table is preceded by a neutral header (\texttt{Table A:}, \texttt{Table B:}, \ldots{}). The first t tables, with t $\in$ \{0, 1, 2, 4\}, are the \textbf{history}. They are complete, and each uses a fresh set of words, so no word is reused across the tables of a trial. The last table is the \textbf{target}, which reveals k of its n$^{2}$ cells, the \textbf{cue}. Every unrevealed target cell is then queried independently by appending a newline and \texttt{wa * wb =}. The answer is a forced choice among the target's n words, scored by the model's next-token log-probability of each word with a leading space.

A single generator produced all stimuli. It assigns fresh words to each table through a random word--element bijection (only the leak control repeats a table, by design), randomises fact order, blacklists numerals, ordinals and identity-suggestive words, and draws from 101 words that are single tokens, with and without a leading space, in every tokenizer used. Because every table carries its own words, a base history can help with the target only through the structure of its tables.

\subsection{Forcing classes}\label{sec:classes}

Every queried cell is labelled exactly with the weakest axiom class under which the cue determines its value. This gives six \textbf{forcing classes}:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Latin-forced (L)}: every Latin square consistent with the cue agrees on the cell.
  \item \textbf{Loop-forced (O)}: every loop consistent with the cue agrees, so identity and cancellation suffice.
  \item \textbf{Associativity-forced / G-forced (G)}: every group table on the same labels agrees; the cell is forced only through associativity.
  \item \textbf{Ab} and \textbf{Cy}: the cell is forced only once commutativity or cyclicity is added.
  \item \textbf{U}: the cell is undetermined.
\end{itemize}

Latin classes were computed by enumeration for n $\leq$ 5 and with a SAT solver~\cite{ignatiev2018pysat} otherwise, loop classes by enumeration for n $\leq$ 6 and SAT otherwise, and group classes by enumerating all labelled tables of every group of order n. The exact learners' code recomputes the classes; it agreed with the stimulus labels on all 57,200 queried cells of the main design (0 mismatches), and SAT agreed with exact counts on 913 trials.

Accuracy on G cells is the primary measure. A G cell is by definition not determined by identity and cancellation, so a learner that uses only Latin or loop constraints can do no better on it than guessing among the values a loop completion of the cue allows (the loop level); only a learner that uses group structure can exceed that level. Accuracy on L cells, $\mathrm{acc}_L$, measures the most basic inference, and chance on every class is 1/n (0.167 at n=6).

\subsection{Conditions}\label{sec:conditions}

The fingerprint compares G-cell accuracy across five history conditions (Table~\ref{tab:conditions}), the base condition and four controls, each of which isolates one route by which a history could raise accuracy.

\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash\hsize=0.4704\hsize}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash\hsize=2.1136\hsize}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash\hsize=0.7530\hsize}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash\hsize=0.6630\hsize}X@{}}
\toprule
condition & history & target & controls for \\
\midrule
base & random groups of order n & random group & --- \\
scramble & Latin squares with no two-sided identity, matched in fact count and token length & random group & context length \\
held-out types & n=6: Z6 only; n=8: abelian types only (Z8, Z4$\times$Z2, Z2$^{3}$) & an unseen type (n=6: S3; n=8: D4 or Q8) & exemplar matching \\

The \textbf{scramble control} contains no group but matches a base history in facts and tokens (6 of the 400 n=6 scramble tables have a one-sided identity). Base minus scramble G accuracy at t=4, written t4 $-$ scramble, therefore measures what group histories add beyond context length. With \textbf{held-out types}, no history table shares the target's isomorphism type, so an exemplar matcher has nothing to copy while an abstracting learner can still apply the axioms. The \textbf{leak control} makes every queried cell answerable by recall, a positive control for context use. The \textbf{loops} condition supplies histories that have an identity but are not associative, testing whether a learner infers ``group'' from an identity alone.

At n=6 (k=10) and n=8 (k=16) the main design covers base t $\in$ \{0, 1, 4\}, scramble t=4 and held-out t $\in$ \{1, 4\}; n=6 alone adds base t=2 and leak t=1. At n=5 (k=6) it covers base t $\in$ \{0, 4\} and the two loop cells at t=4. With 100 trials per cell, every idealised learner, pretrained model and trained network sees the same 1,800 trials and 57,200 scored cells (the In-Context Algebra model sees only the cells that fit its 16-symbol vocabulary, Section~\ref{sec:ica}). The order n=6 is primary and n=8 secondary.

\subsection{Idealised learners}\label{sec:learners}

To check that the fingerprint separates the hypotheses it targets, we scored seven exact algorithms on the identical trials:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{R} recalls only.
  \item \textbf{N} chooses uniformly among the Latin-feasible values and otherwise ignores the history; like every other preregistered learner, it first copies a cell that appears verbatim in the history (R does only this), which is possible only in the leak control.
  \item \textbf{N\_iso} matches the cue against the history tables up to relabelling (exemplar matching), with a Latin fallback.
  \item \textbf{A} induces axioms (identity, associativity, commutativity, cyclicity) from the history tables, then applies them.
  \item \textbf{Asl} is like A, but infers ``group'' from an identity alone.
  \item \textbf{B} is Bayes-optimal under the true environment prior.
  \item \textbf{Bh} is hierarchical Bayes over the Latin, loop, group, abelian and cyclic environments.
\end{itemize}

Ties are broken uniformly at random with a fixed seed. The rule distinguishes five learner classes: \textbf{R} (no inference), \textbf{N} (inference without use of the history), \textbf{N\_iso} (exemplar reuse), \textbf{A} (abstraction) and \textbf{B-type} (the structural prior is in place without history). The preregistered G-cell predictions at n=6, k=10 differ sharply. R stays at chance (0.17) and N at 0.30 for every t. N\_iso rises gradually (0.30, 0.65 and 0.96 at t = 0, 1 and 4), with held-out accuracy near 0.31. A steps from 0.30 at t=0 to 1.00 from t=1, with held-out accuracy 1.00. B and Bh stay at or near 1.00. Abstraction and exemplar matching therefore both compound to near ceiling by $t = 4$, so the compounding contrast alone cannot tell them apart; in the rule, held-out transfer does, and the shape statistic (Section~\ref{sec:rule}) adds a secondary step-versus-gradual distinction.

An eighth learner, \textbf{C (count shortcut)}, was added \emph{post hoc}, after the trained networks were found to use it (Section~\ref{sec:r-trained}). C answers uniformly among the target words that occur least often as a result in the revealed cue. It uses no cell-level, history or axiom information.

\subsection{Decision rule}\label{sec:rule}

The decision rule (Table~\ref{tab:rule}) was \emph{preregistered} and frozen before any model output. It is applied per model to the n=6 cells, on accuracy and, separately, on mean $p_{\mathrm{gold}}$, the probability of the correct word under a softmax over the n candidates.

\begin{table}[tbp]
\centering
\small
\caption{The preregistered decision rule, applied in order; the first step whose criterion holds assigns the class. G t0, G t4, G scr4 and G held4 are G-cell accuracies at base t=0, base t=4, scramble t=4 and held-out t=4.}\label{tab:rule}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}l>{\raggedright\arraybackslash\hsize=1.9520\hsize}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash\hsize=0.6774\hsize}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash\hsize=0.3706\hsize}X@{}}
\toprule
step & quantity & criterion & class \\
\midrule
1 & $\mathrm{acc}_L$, L-cell accuracy at base t=0 & $\mathrm{acc}_L < 1/n + 0.25$ & R \\
2 & rescaling $g(x) = (x - 1/n)/(\mathrm{acc}_L - 1/n)$ & --- & --- \\
3 & g(G t0) & $\geq 0.85$ & B-type \\
4 & base = max(g(G t0), g(G scr4)); comp = g(G t4) $-$ base & comp $<$ 0.15 & N \\
5 & held = g(G held4) $-$ base & held $\geq$ 0.6$\cdot$comp & A; otherwise N\_iso \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

Step 1 asks whether the model infers at all: below 1/n + 0.25 (0.417 at n=6), even cells that the Latin property alone determines are not solved, and the model is class R. Step 2 rescales accuracy so that 0 is chance and 1 is the model's own Latin accuracy. Step 3 identifies a learner whose group prior is already in place at t=0. Step 4 takes the higher of the t=0 and scramble values as baseline, so that a gain from context length alone does not count as compounding. Step 5 asks whether the gain survives when no history table shares the target's type.

The rule always also reports the abstraction fraction $w$ = held/comp and the shape statistic g(G t4) $-$ g(G t1). A shape near 0 indicates a step, as for A; N\_iso's gradual rise gives about 0.3. At n=8 the same quantities form a secondary analysis, with raw G accuracy reported alongside, because L cells are rare there (fewer than 40 per cell) and $\mathrm{acc}_L$ is noisy. For class R the rescaled quantities are not meaningful, since g is undefined when $\mathrm{acc}_L$ is near chance; class R means only that $\mathrm{acc}_L$ is below threshold, and recall is read separately from the leak control. Applied to the idealised learners, the rule returns each learner's own class at both n=6 and n=8, on both accuracy and mean $p_{\mathrm{gold}}$, with 0 misclassifications; Asl is classified A (Section~\ref{sec:r-ideal}).

\section{Experimental setup}\label{sec:setup}

All model inference and training ran on one shared laptop RTX 5070 GPU (8 GB); the exact learners and analyses ran on the CPU.

\subsection{Models and scoring}\label{sec:models}

We scored nine checkpoints (ten model--precision configurations) from three families (Table~\ref{tab:models}): Qwen3~\cite{qwen3}, base and post-trained; SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct~\cite{smollm2}, a Llama-architecture model; and the fully open OLMo-2~\cite{olmo2}.

Prompts are the raw context plus the query, without a chat template. Queries were batched on copies of each trial's prefix cache rather than scored singly as preregistered; on the Experiment-1 models the two agree on 94--98\% of argmax decisions, differing only on near-ties. For the 7B and 8B models, embeddings and the float32 output head ran on the CPU; in two checks this offload agreed with standard scoring on 91.9\% and 94.7\% of argmax decisions. Some result files mix revisions of the scoring script (Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}). Re-scoring the four n=6 cells of Qwen3-1.7B-Base's primary contrast with the final code, one query at a time, moved per-cell G accuracy by at most 0.005 and left t4 $-$ scramble at $-$0.006 [$-$0.034, +0.021] (originally $-$0.007 [$-$0.037, +0.020]; Appendix~\ref{app:impl}).

nf4 quantisation~\cite{dettmers2023qlora} was needed to fit the 4B, 7B and 8B models. A \emph{preregistered} bf16-versus-nf4 control on Qwen3-1.7B-Base required an unchanged class and every per-cell G accuracy within 0.03. \textbf{The control failed.} nf4 lowered G accuracy in all 17 cells that contain G queries, by 0.020--0.067, and per-query argmax agreement was 56\%, although the class (R at n=6 and n=8) and the null t4 $-$ scramble contrast were unchanged (Section~\ref{sec:r-llm}). As preregistered, all nf4 results, marked \textsuperscript{\dag}, carry the caveat that G accuracy is biased low by about 0.04 and per-query predictions are unstable. The control shows that nf4 did not create an effect, not that it could not hide a weak one.

\subsection{Calibration}\label{sec:calib}

Because compounding presupposes Latin inference, Experiment 2a swept cue density (n=6, base histories, t $\in$ \{0, 4\}, k $\in$ \{6, 10, 16, 22, 28\}, 50 new trials per (t, k)) on eight models. The Latin threshold $k_L$ is the smallest k at which L accuracy, pooled over t, reaches 0.5; a model without one is \emph{non-inferential} on this format.

A guard requiring at least 30 pooled L queries per k, added after the Qwen3-0.6B-Base sweep because k=6 has only 4 L cells in 100 trials, changes the status of two models. Without it, Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base answer 2 of 4 L queries at k=6, so $k_L = 6$; being R at k=10, they trigger the preregistered conditional step (addendum 2d), the only adaptive step allowed, which regenerates the n=6 main contrasts at k=16 (100 trials per cell, new seeds) and takes $\mathrm{acc}_L$ from k=16 base t=0. We ran it as specified after the final audit and report both readings (Section~\ref{sec:r-cal}).

Two \emph{exploratory} variants are not used for classification: an instructed task header (k $\in$ \{10, 22\}) and a sorted format that lists the target's facts by row (k $\in$ \{16, 22, 28\}), added after the first three $\leq$1.7B models showed chance-level L accuracy. As \emph{post hoc} references we computed learner C and one-pass row/column elimination, which guesses uniformly among the values absent from the cell's row and column.

\subsection{Transformers trained from scratch}\label{sec:trained}

To test whether the fingerprint recovers the class implied by a known training diet (Experiment 3), we trained GPT-style decoders (pre-LN, rotary embeddings~\cite{su2021rope}, width 256, 8 heads, 1, 2, 4 or 6 layers; 3.17M parameters at 4 layers) on in-context group-table sequences laid out like the stimuli, in a 70-token vocabulary with fresh symbols per table and loss on answer tokens only. Diets use orders \{4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10\} and exclude S3, D4 and Q8. The mixed-environment diet (A1, A2, A4, A6, by layer count) draws each sequence from groups (0.5), identity-free Latin squares (0.25) or non-associative loops (0.25), so that history is informative about the environment. Three 4-layer controls use groups only (G4), groups from a fixed pool of 32 labelled tables per order (P4), and an exemplar diet of isomorphic-copy tasks and identity-free Latin squares with no group or identity (I4).

Predicted classes were frozen before training (Section~\ref{sec:r-trained}). The method counts as validated if A4 is A or B-type, I4 is N\_iso, and P4 and A1 are R or N; a run whose in-training remaining-fact accuracy at n=6 never exceeds chance + 0.10 is \emph{not learned} and excluded from validation.

Training ran for 14,000 AdamW steps~\cite{loshchilov2019adamw} ($\beta$ = 0.9/0.95, weight decay 0.1, clipping 1.0, seed 0) of $\lfloor 65536/L \rfloor$ sequences of length L, each step from a single (n, t), with 500 warmup steps and cosine decay to 10\% of a $6 \times 10^{-4}$ peak ($10^{-3}$ for 1--2 layers); t $\in$ 0--4 (t $\leq$ 2 at n=10, so that sequences fit 2,400 tokens). The target table is complete in training and the loss covers every answer token after the sequence's first fact, so the generator's cue size k, uniform in $[\lceil 0.15 n^{2} \rceil, \lfloor 0.45 n^{2} \rfloor]$, does not affect training. Four runs were interrupted by laptop standby or a scheduler change; three were resumed from their last checkpoint and one retrained from scratch, all reaching the preregistered 14,000 steps on a continuous learning-rate schedule (Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}).

Each network was scored on the identical Experiment-1 trials, with words mapped to fresh random symbols per table (four draws), and classified by the unchanged rule; a \emph{post hoc} diagnostic compares its predictions with learner C and cell-level row/column elimination.

\subsection{Reasoning probe}\label{sec:probe}

Experiment 4 (\emph{exploratory}, not preregistered) asked whether direct answering limits Latin inference. Qwen3-1.7B answered one Latin-forced cell per trial under a chat prompt stating the Latin-square rule, so the probe measures inference given the rule. Decoding was greedy, with thinking on (at most 4,096 tokens) or off (at most 400); truncated thinking counts as incorrect. The planned design (four conditions $\times$ 30 trials, 1,536 thinking tokens) truncated all 13 thinking answers in its first condition, so we reduced it to 15 trials each of sorted and raw k=28.

\subsection{The CR axis}\label{sec:cr}

Experiment 5 (\emph{preregistered}) tested the ``compute versus retrieve'' activation detector from our earlier preprint~\cite{ramdan2026cr}, whose stated limitation is that its compute prompts are longer and more complex than its retrieval prompts. Our stimuli remove this confound: in the n=6 leak cell at t=1 every query is retrievable, while in base at t=1 the same format, token count and query position require inference.

We ran the published detector code read-only, in bf16 rather than fp16: a mean-difference axis from the paper's 30 + 30 calibration prompts at the best of four layers, read at the last token of chat-template (primary) and raw inputs. The three bf16 models received all 26 queries per trial and the two nf4 models (\textsuperscript{\dag}) 11--12 class-stratified queries, over 100 trials per condition. On Qwen3-0.6B-Base (bf16, uncached forwards) our forward pass reproduced the detector's hidden states exactly; the nf4 and CPU-embedding paths were not checked this way, and the cached path matched uncached forwards in an audit check (r $\geq$ 0.996; Appendix~\ref{app:impl}). H1 predicts that base projects higher, toward ``compute'', than leak; it is supported if the trial-bootstrap CI excludes 0 in that direction in at least 3 of 5 models. H2 predicts a rise in the order L $<$ O $<$ G within base. The hypotheses were finalised minutes after a discarded 6-trial smoke test whose estimate pointed against H1; the direction was kept.

Experiment 5b (\emph{exploratory}) followed the H1 result and a 20-trial audit pilot in which relabelling closed 53\% and 71\% of the gap, so it re-estimates a seen effect rather than testing it independently. Leak and base are matched in length and format but not vocabulary: a leak context has 6 distinct words, a base context 12 (Appendix~\ref{app:cr}). \textbf{baseRel} writes the base history in the target's words (shared vocabulary, still non-retrievable); \textbf{leakRel} permutes the leak history's words by a random derangement (identical vocabulary, inconsistent answers). We report $f_{\mathrm{vocab}} = (\mathrm{baseRel} - \mathrm{base})/(\mathrm{leak} - \mathrm{base})$, the share of the gap reproduced by vocabulary alone, and leakRel $-$ leak, retrievability with vocabulary fixed (predicted $>$ 0), from uncached forwards on all 26 queries and 100 trials in four models.

\subsection{Positive control}\label{sec:ica}

Experiment 6 (\emph{preregistered}) applied the fingerprint to the released In-Context Algebra model~\cite{todd2026ica}, a real network that should not be class R: a 4-layer, 8-head transformer with d=1024 and 16 symbol tokens, trained on in-context cyclic and dihedral group tables (C3--C10, D2--D5). We re-implemented it from the released code without executing that code.

On its own distribution the port reaches 0.973 held-out final-fact accuracy, and 0.959 under the upstream protocol on 1,024 fresh sequences, against the authors' 99.4\%. Theirs is the best of about 290 training-time evaluations on one cached 512-sequence set; on our fresh sequences the released checkpoints from 20k steps on score 0.959--0.975, so the gap is consistent with checkpoint selection rather than a port error. Training loss is 0.917 (upstream: about 0.93), and an independent second forward pass agrees with the adapter on 3,200 of 3,200 answer positions (Appendix~\ref{app:ica}).

The adapter maps each trial's words to distinct random symbols (four draws; no group identity maps to `0', as in training) and scores each query by forced choice over the target's n symbols. Only cells with at most 16 distinct words fit, which excludes every t $\geq$ 2 and scramble cell, so comp, held and w cannot be computed. The primary analysis is therefore rule steps 1--3 on base t=0, returning R, B-type or ``non-R, non-B'', with six directional predictions (Section~\ref{sec:r-ica}). Interleaved fact order and six training checkpoints are \emph{exploratory}; a mechanism split of G cells, compared with an exact loop-level baseline, is \emph{post hoc}.

\subsection{Statistics, preregistration and audits}\label{sec:stats}

Accuracies carry Wilson 95\% intervals, except the rule's $\mathrm{acc}_L$ intervals, which are trial-bootstrap percentile intervals. Contrasts carry trial-level bootstrap 95\% intervals (2,000 resamples within each cell), with seeds fixed per test in the main analyses; only the Experiment 2 per-model t4 $-$ t0 CIs and the scoring re-check depend on processing order.

Experiments 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 were \emph{preregistered} (2026-10-06 to 2026-10-11), each before its outputs, except that Experiment 5's file was finalised minutes after a discarded six-trial smoke test; Experiments 4 and 5b are \emph{exploratory}. We report every model and run, including nulls and interrupted runs. Two adversarial audits re-derived the Experiment 1--5 numbers that existed at the time; later verification passes (2026-10-09 to 2026-10-11) re-derived the results produced after them (learner C, the count-shortcut diagnostic, the scoring checks, Experiment 5b and the addendum-2d run) and those of Experiment 6. All corrections are incorporated. Appendix~\ref{app:deviations} lists all 23 deviations, including 100 rather than 200 trials per cell. Apart from the $\geq$30-query guard, none altered a stimulus, threshold or decision rule.

\section{Results}\label{sec:results}

Every run is complete. All numbers below come from auto-generated result tables, and the full table for every model, network and idealised learner except Asl is in Appendix~\ref{app:main}. Two adversarial audits re-derived the Experiment 1--5 numbers that existed at the time, and later verification passes (2026-10-09 to 2026-10-11) re-derived the results produced after them and those of Experiment 6; the text incorporates all their corrections. Post hoc and exploratory analyses are labelled where they appear, and every deviation from the preregistrations is listed in Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}.

\subsection{The fingerprint separates the idealised learners}\label{sec:r-ideal}

We scored the seven preregistered exact learners (Section~\ref{sec:learners}) on the same 1,800 trials that the models see. The preregistered decision rule (Section~\ref{sec:rule}) returns every learner's own class at n=6 and at n=8, on both accuracy and mean $p_{\mathrm{gold}}$, with 0 misclassifications; Asl, which infers ``group'' from an identity alone, is classified A. Table~\ref{tab:learners} lists the signatures at n=6.

On associativity-forced (G) cells the four core signatures differ sharply (Figure~\ref{fig:ideal}). The notebook learner N stays flat, at 0.29 at t=0, 0.28 at t=4 and 0.29 on held-out types. Exemplar matching (N\_iso) rises gradually, through 0.30, 0.69, 0.85 and 0.98 at t = 0, 1, 2 and 4, but stays at 0.30 on held-out types; its shape statistic is +0.35 [+0.26, +0.45] and its $w$ is about 0. Abstraction (A) steps to 1.00 at t=1 and keeps that level on held-out types, with a shape of 0.000 and $w$ = 1.00. Bayes with the true prior (B) is at 1.00 from t=0. B and Bh are classified B-type at step 3, before the compounding contrast is consulted.

The compounding contrast, t=4 minus a length-matched scramble history, is about +0.70 for both A and N\_iso. Only held-out transfer separates them cleanly: held-out minus scramble is +0.70 for A against +0.03 for N\_iso. A compounding contrast on its own therefore cannot tell abstraction from exemplar reuse, and the held-out types are what make the distinction.

At n=8, N\_iso's G accuracy (0.22, 0.46 and 0.59 at t = 0, 1 and 4) tracks the missing mass realised in these stimuli: the target type occurs in the history in 28\% of trials at t=1 and 47\% at t=4. It departs from the design-stage expected-coverage prediction (0.38 and 0.69) because the sampled histories over-cover the target type at t=1 (expected 20\%) and under-cover it at t=4 (expected 59\%).

\textbf{Post hoc.} We added an eighth learner, C (count shortcut), after the diagnosis reported in Section~\ref{sec:r-trained}. It answers with the target word least represented among the revealed facts. The rule classifies it R at n=6 and at n=8, with $\mathrm{acc}_L$ 0.175, G t0 0.226 and leak 0.235. This is the correct verdict, because C uses no cell-level, history or axiom information.

\subsection{Pretrained models are recall-only and do not compound}\label{sec:r-llm}

All nine checkpoints (ten model--precision configurations) from three families are classified R at both n=6 and n=8, on both accuracy and $p_{\mathrm{gold}}$ (Table~\ref{tab:recall}). The set comprises the post-trained Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B; Qwen3-0.6B-Base, Qwen3-1.7B-Base (bf16 and nf4\textsuperscript{\dag}), Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base (nf4\textsuperscript{\dag})~\cite{qwen3}; SmolLM2-1.7B, which has a Llama architecture~\cite{smollm2}; and OLMo-2-1B (bf16) and OLMo-2-7B (nf4\textsuperscript{\dag}), a fully open family~\cite{olmo2}. Accuracy on Latin-forced cells at t=0 ($\mathrm{acc}_L$) is 0.14--0.29. Several values are at or below chance (0.167), and every value is below the preregistered threshold of 0.417.

\paragraph{No compounding}

At n=6, t4 $-$ scramble lies between $-$0.019 and +0.026 (Qwen3-8B-Base: $-$0.008 [$-$0.038, +0.022]), and every 95\% CI includes 0 (Figure~\ref{fig:llm}). Held-out minus scramble lies between $-$0.04 and +0.02.

Two raw increases from t=0 to t=4 were reliable, and both vanish against the scramble history. OLMo-2-1B at n=6 gains +0.042 [+0.011, +0.073] from t=0 to t=4, but only +0.020 [$-$0.008, +0.051] relative to scramble. Qwen3-0.6B at n=8 gains +0.031 [+0.014, +0.048], and +0.008 relative to scramble, with a CI that includes 0. Neither raw gain survives the length-matched control, so both are consistent with effects of context length alone, which is why that control is needed.

\paragraph{Recall depends on family more than on size}

When the history contains the target's own labelled table (the leak control), G-cell accuracy is 0.52--0.65 for the Qwen3 models up to 1.7B (0.59 for nf4 Qwen3-1.7B-Base), 0.95 for Qwen3-4B-Base and 0.96 for Qwen3-8B-Base. It is 0.44 for SmolLM2-1.7B, and 0.31 and 0.37 for OLMo-2-1B and OLMo-2-7B. The larger Qwen3 models thus retrieve almost perfectly and still do not infer.

\paragraph{Quantisation control (\textsuperscript{\dag})}

The preregistered control (Qwen3-1.7B-Base, nf4 against bf16, all 1,800 trials) \emph{failed} its tolerance. nf4 lowered G accuracy in all 17 cells that contain G queries, by 0.020--0.067 (pooled $-$0.034; mean of per-cell differences $-$0.040), and per-query argmax agreement was 56\%. The class (R) is unchanged, and the compounding contrast is null in both precisions: at n=6, t4 $-$ scramble is $-$0.007 [$-$0.037, +0.020] in bf16 and +0.006 [$-$0.022, +0.035] in nf4.

nf4 therefore did not create a spurious effect, and it preserved strong context use (leak 0.63 $\to$ 0.59). What this control cannot show is whether nf4 would hide a weak real effect at 4B, 7B or 8B, because at 1.7B there was nothing to hide. The low bias (pooled $-$0.034) applies to G accuracy; pooled L accuracy moved by $-$0.024 and O accuracy by +0.032.

\paragraph{Answer bias (post hoc)}

A post-hoc diagnostic (\texttt{exp1/\allowbreak{}diag.py}) shows that at n=6 Qwen3-1.7B and SmolLM2-1.7B answer G cells with one of the query's own words in 46\% and 44\% of cases, against 30\% for a uniform guess; over all orders the shares are 39\% and 40\%, against 26\%. Qwen3-0.6B shows no such bias at n=6 (27\% against 30\%) or at n=8 (14\% against 23\%; 19\% against 26\% over all orders). At n=5, however, it too exceeds the uniform rate (46\% against 35\%), and the two 1.7B models score 62\% and 56\%. Because the correct answer is never a query word (0 of 31,553 G cells), this bias pulls G accuracy below chance.

Two pretrained models rise marginally. For Qwen3-8B-Base the rise appears at both t=0 (0.22 $\to$ 0.29) and t=4 (0.14 $\to$ 0.23), but neither per-t CI excludes 0, and at k=28 accuracy is lower with four history tables than with none (0.23 against 0.29). OLMo-2-7B starts below chance, at 0.12, and its rise is concentrated at t=0.

\paragraph{The Latin threshold and the conditional k=16 step}

At k=6 there are only 4 L queries in 100 trials, and Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base each answer 2 of them correctly (0.50). Under the addendum-2a rule as frozen, that makes $k_L$ = 6 for these two models. Both are R at k=10, so the conditional k=16 operating point (addendum 2d) is triggered. The guard of at least 30 L queries, which excluded k=6, was added after the Qwen3-0.6B-Base sweep had been seen (Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}, row 4). We therefore also ran 2d as preregistered, on 2026-10-09, after the final audit. Both models remain R at k=16. Their $\mathrm{acc}_L$ values are 0.177 [0.154, 0.201] and 0.219 [0.196, 0.241] (trial-bootstrap 95\% CIs, as computed by the decision rule), below 0.417, and t4 $-$ scramble is $-$0.034 [$-$0.092, +0.024] and +0.006 [$-$0.058, +0.065].

With the guard, $k_L$ is undefined for all eight calibrated models, so all of them are \emph{non-inferential} on this format. Qwen3-0.6B, the post-trained model, was not swept.

\paragraph{Missing information does not explain the failure (post hoc)}

At k=28, 98\% of the missing cells are Latin-forced (784 of 800), and one-pass row/column elimination alone leaves a single candidate for 86\% of those (675 of 784; \texttt{exp2/\allowbreak{}k28\_elimination.md}). Choosing uniformly among the remaining candidates, this elimination would score 0.92 over all missing cells. The direct-answer failure is therefore not about missing information.

\paragraph{Sorted format (exploratory)}

Listing the target's facts row by row, a variant added after the sweeps of the first three models (Qwen3-0.6B-Base, Qwen3-1.7B and SmolLM2-1.7B; Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}), helps at k=28. Qwen3-4B-Base gains +0.108 [+0.066, +0.149] and Qwen3-8B-Base +0.101 [+0.061, +0.144], reaching 0.32 and 0.36. Smaller gains with CIs excluding 0 appear for Qwen3-1.7B-Base (+0.046), OLMo-2-7B (+0.045) and Qwen3-0.6B-Base (+0.029). Qwen3-1.7B (+0.027) and SmolLM2-1.7B (+0.024) show similar but non-significant gains, and OLMo-2-1B shows none (+0.005). Sorted-format gains are therefore not specific to 8B (Appendix~\ref{app:calib}).

\paragraph{Instructed header (exploratory)}

A one-paragraph task header changed L and G accuracy by $-$0.083 to +0.042 over 32 contrasts: 8 models $\times$ k $\in$ \{10, 22\} $\times$ \{L, G\}, pooled over t. Each contrast requires at least 30 queries in its cell. This guard was added to the $k_L$ rule after the first sweep (Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}, row 4), and it is applied here to every class. The mean change is $-$0.006, and 2 of the 32 CIs exclude 0, both negative.

\paragraph{Experiment-2 hypotheses}

The preregistered H1, that L accuracy rises with k for every model, is not supported. Its second part, that $k_L$ falls with scale, cannot be tested with the guard; without it, only two of the smallest models have a $k_L$, an artefact of 4 queries. H2, that any compounding appears only in the larger models, holds vacuously, since no model compounds. H3, that held-out transfer separates A from N\_iso in a model that compounds, cannot be tested.

\subsection{Trained transformers learn a counting shortcut}\label{sec:r-trained}

We trained seven GPT-style networks from scratch on the preregistered diets (Section~\ref{sec:trained}), with 3.2M parameters at 4 layers and about 0.91B training tokens each (14,000 steps of up to 65,536 tokens). Every one is classified R, and every one also fails the recall (leak) control, with leak G accuracy of 0.08--0.24 (Table~\ref{tab:app-main-class}). For these networks, class R means only that $\mathrm{acc}_L$ is below threshold: they neither recall nor infer at sparse cues.

\paragraph{Diagnosis (post hoc)}

The learned networks answer each trial with essentially one word: the target word least represented among the revealed facts (\texttt{exp3/\allowbreak{}heur/\allowbreak{}}). In A4, 98.6\% of predictions fall in that least-revealed set, which across cells holds about 30\% of the target words. A4's accuracy equals that of the count shortcut C to within 0.001 on all 1,800 main trials ($-$0.0008 [$-$0.0017, +0.0001]) and on the cue sweep, and A1, A2, G4 and I4 match C to within 0.007.

The shortcut also explains the in-training plateau. Applied to the in-training evaluation conditions (teacher-forced, with the training generator), the count shortcut scores 0.33 at n=6 and 0.25 at n=8, and the networks reach 0.29--0.36 at step 14,000. On the identical sequences, averaged over the evaluation conditions of each order, A4, G4 and I4 sit within $\pm$0.006 of the shortcut, A1 and A2 sit below it, and A6 sits slightly above it (+0.015 at n=6). Cell-level row/column elimination would score 0.70.

It also explains A4's rise on the cue sweep. On L cells A4 goes from 0.17 at k=10 through 0.21 and 0.26 to 0.33 at k=28 (Table~\ref{tab:cal}). Over all cells its accuracy matches the shortcut's to within 0.004 at every k: 0.196 against 0.200 at k=6, 0.214 against 0.213 at k=10, and 0.334 against 0.334 at k=28. The networks therefore did not learn Latin constraints. They learned a global symbol-count statistic, which is a weak consequence of the Latin property.

Among the learned networks, the 6-layer A6 is the only exception, and a small one. It is less constant within a trial (75\% of its predictions fall in the least-revealed set), and it beats the shortcut by +0.014 [+0.012, +0.015]. P4, which is not learned, does not follow the shortcut at all: 28\% of its predictions fall in the least-revealed set, about the uniform rate, and its accuracy is 0.048 below the shortcut's.

Two entries need a note. A2 was predicted to be N-like with O $\gg$ G, but at n=6, t=0 its O and G accuracies are 0.21 and 0.22. A6 has $w$ = 0.57, but the value is uninterpretable because its comp is negative ($-$0.22), and A4's $w$ is undefined.

\paragraph{Learning-failure rule (preregistered)}

We applied the three preregistered Experiment-3 criteria (\texttt{exp3/\allowbreak{}PREREGISTRATION.md}) after the second audit. Under the learning-failure rule, every run except P4 exceeds chance + 0.10 (0.267) on in-training n=6 remaining-fact accuracy, with maxima of 0.33--0.36. P4 never does: its maximum is 0.183, and it memorised its pool (training loss 0.005) without transfer to fresh symbols. P4 is therefore \emph{not learned}; we report it but exclude it from method validation. A post-hoc caveat applies: the count shortcut alone scores 0.33, so this threshold does not distinguish learning the task from learning the shortcut. A future preregistration should set the threshold relative to learner C.

\paragraph{Method validation: not met}

A4 and I4 are R, against predictions of A or B-type and of N\_iso. The preregistration asks that each mismatch be attributed either to the method or to the training diet. The in-training evaluations, compared post hoc with the count shortcut, attribute it to training. On the identical training-generator sequences, A4 and I4 stay, on average over conditions, within $\pm$0.006 of the count shortcut at n=6 and n=8. Their first-fact accuracy after the cue (0.23 for A4 and 0.21 for I4 at step 14,000; chance 0.17) is near the shortcut's level (0.20) and well below row/column elimination (0.30). On the identical trials, the fingerprint returns the same class (R) for the networks as for the exact count learner C.

\paragraph{Depth: not supported}

Held-out G accuracy at t=4 is 0.230 (A1), 0.226 (A2), 0.238 (A4) and 0.239 (A6). This is not monotone in depth, and the CIs overlap. comp is undefined for A1, A2 and A4, because their $\mathrm{acc}_L$ is below chance; for A6 it is negative, $-$0.22 [$-$3.24, +0.16].

\subsection{Reasoning probe (exploratory)}\label{sec:r-probe}

This probe was exploratory and not preregistered (Section~\ref{sec:probe}). Qwen3-1.7B answered Latin-forced cells with thinking on (up to 4,096 tokens) and off. The trials were the first 15 t=0 trials each of the sorted and raw k=28 formats, and the prompt stated the Latin rule. With thinking off, the model answered 4 of 15 sorted and 3 of 15 raw trials correctly. With thinking on, it answered 1 of 15 correctly in each format, and 14 of the 15 runs in each format were truncated.

In all, 28 of the 30 thinking runs hit the token budget. Both runs that finished (2,604 and 3,453 tokens) were correct, but paired by trial, no trial is correct only with thinking on. In an earlier run with a 1,536-token budget, all 13 thinking answers were truncated. Six of the 30 non-thinking answers also reached their 400-token limit without an ANSWER line (sorted trials 6 and 8; raw trials 4, 6, 8 and 12). They were scored by the last candidate word mentioned, and all six were incorrect.

The probe is dominated by truncation. It neither shows nor excludes reasoning-enabled Latin inference at this scale.

\subsection{The compute--retrieve axis under matched format}\label{sec:r-cr}

The compute--retrieve detector~\cite{ramdan2026cr} separates its own calibration prompts well in every model we tested, with AUC 0.96--0.99 at the chosen layer (Section~\ref{sec:cr}). On the fingerprint stimuli, queries in the leak condition at t=1 are retrievable, and queries in the base condition at t=1 must be inferred. Format, token count and query position are identical across the two. Behaviour differs sharply: accuracy over the queried cells is 0.53--0.97 in leak and 0.17--0.22 in base (0.17--0.21 on the subset of queries projected in Experiment 5).

The preregistered H1, that base projects higher than leak (toward ``compute'') in the detector format, is supported in 0 of 5 models, against a criterion of at least 3 (Table~\ref{tab:cr}). In three models the difference is significant in the \emph{opposite} direction. This outcome lies outside the preregistered interpretations, which covered only ``supported'' and ``not supported''. H2, that projection rises from L to O to G cells within base, is null in four models and significantly reversed in Qwen3-1.7B-Base ($\rho$ = $-$0.113 [$-$0.176, $-$0.046]). In an exploratory analysis, projection also does not predict correctness within a condition (AUC 0.46--0.55, except 0.38 in Qwen3-1.7B-Base leak).

In raw format, without the chat template (exploratory), the sign changes. Base exceeds leak, with the CI excluding 0, in Qwen3-0.6B-Base, Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base, which would meet the 3-of-5 criterion had raw format been primary. Base falls below leak in Qwen3-1.7B (d = $-$0.28) and Qwen3-8B-Base (d = $-$1.68).

\paragraph{Context vocabulary (Experiment 5b; exploratory, not preregistered)}

Leak and base are matched on length and format, but not on vocabulary. Leak contexts reuse the target's 6 words in the history, while base histories use 6 other words. Leak contexts therefore have half the vocabulary, about 5$\times$ more occurrences of the query words, and a verbatim copy of every target line. The control changes only the history table (100 trials per model, all 26 queries, uncached forwards; Appendix~\ref{app:cr}). In \textbf{baseRel} the history stays non-retrievable but is written in the target's words. In \textbf{leakRel} the history keeps leak's vocabulary but its answers are deranged, so retrievability is the only difference from leak.

Vocabulary explains most of the reversal. In the three base models reversed in detector format, baseRel reproduces 64--87\% of the base--leak gap: $f_{\mathrm{vocab}}$ is 0.67 [0.54, 0.85] for Qwen3-0.6B-Base, 0.87 [0.79, 0.96] for Qwen3-1.7B-Base and 0.64 [0.40, 0.99] for Qwen3-4B-Base (Figure~\ref{fig:cr}).

With vocabulary fixed (leakRel $-$ leak, predicted $>$ 0), the sign depends on model and wrapper. In detector format the contrast is reversed in Qwen3-0.6B-Base ($d_z$ $-$0.36) and Qwen3-1.7B-Base ($-$0.28), null in Qwen3-4B-Base ($-$0.10), and in the predicted direction only in the post-trained Qwen3-1.7B (+0.36). In raw format it is in the predicted direction in all four models ($d_z$ +0.33 to +1.67), although at other layers the sign varies.

The post-trained null is a cancellation. In Qwen3-1.7B, vocabulary overlap raises the projection (baseRel $-$ base = +1.8) about as much as retrievability lowers it (leak $-$ leakRel = $-$1.3), which is why the preregistered contrast is null there.

The axis therefore carries an in-context retrieval signal of the predicted sign in two places. In the post-trained model it is small ($d_z$ +0.36 in detector format), about the size of that model's vocabulary effect. In raw format it ranges from $d_z$ +0.33 to +1.67, and in Qwen3-1.7B-Base it exceeds the vocabulary effect. In the base models under the detector's chat template, by contrast, the vocabulary effect (baseRel $-$ base) is 4--12$\times$ the retrievability contrast, and with vocabulary held fixed the retrievability contrast itself is reversed in Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base and null in Qwen3-4B-Base.

\subsection{Positive control: the In-Context Algebra model}\label{sec:r-ica}

The In-Context Algebra study~\cite{todd2026ica} released a 4-layer, d=1024 transformer trained on in-context cyclic and dihedral group tables. We re-implemented it from the released code and scored the released checkpoint on every cell whose trial fits its 16 symbol tokens (Section~\ref{sec:ica}). A second, independent forward pass agrees with our adapter on 3,200 of 3,200 answer positions. On fresh samples of its own task the model scores 0.97 with shuffled vocabulary and 0.959 under the upstream evaluation protocol. The latter is below the 99.4\% the authors report, which is the best of about 290 evaluations on one fixed 512-sequence set; on our fresh sequences, the released checkpoints from 20k steps on score 0.959--0.975. Full-sequence training loss is 0.917, against about 0.93 upstream (Appendix~\ref{app:ica}).

Only cells with t $\leq$ 1 fit the model's vocabulary, so the compounding contrast cannot be measured. Decision-rule steps 1--3 need only the base t=0 cell, and this primary analysis was frozen before scoring (\texttt{exp6/\allowbreak{}PREREGISTRATION.md}).

The model is neither R nor B-type. At n=6, $\mathrm{acc}_L$ is 0.886 [0.820, 0.944], against a threshold of 0.417, and loop-forced cells score 0.91. Associativity-only (G) cells score 0.637 [0.601, 0.675], so g(G t0) = 0.65 [0.59, 0.74], below the B-type threshold of 0.85. The same holds at n=8 ($\mathrm{acc}_L$ 0.971, G 0.663), at n=5 (0.982 and 0.531), on the addendum-2d k=16 stimuli (0.920 and 0.704) and on $p_{\mathrm{gold}}$ (Table~\ref{tab:ica}; Figure~\ref{fig:ica}). In every non-leak cell of the main design (base $t = 0$ at $n = 5$, 6 and 8; base and held-out $t = 1$ at $n = 6$ and 8), O $-$ G is +0.27 to +0.45; on the addendum-2d $k = 16$ stimuli the gap is smaller, +0.20 to +0.22.

This is the first real network for which the fingerprint returns a class above R. Its profile is consistent with its authors' mechanistic analysis: identity, cancellation and copying are near ceiling, and associativity is weakest.

Four of the preregistered predictions are met: the model is not R; leak recall is 1.000; G accuracy exceeds learner C (+0.411 [+0.369, +0.453], paired); and a differently labelled history brings no benefit (t1 $-$ t0 on G: $-$0.025 [$-$0.071, +0.024]). Two are \emph{not met}. The model is not B-type, and G accuracy is not lower on the order-8 types held out from its training (+0.025 [$-$0.035, +0.085]). Accuracy depends on the specific group more than on whether it was seen: Z2$^{3}$ scores 0.97 (its smaller relative Z2$\times$Z2 was in training), and Q8 scores 0.51.

On the t=0 cue sweep, the model's accuracy over all cells rises from 0.69 at k=6 to 0.998 at k=28. On the same trials, Qwen3-8B-Base goes from 0.20 to 0.29, learner C from 0.20 to 0.33, and one-pass row/column elimination from 0.24 to 0.93.

\paragraph{Fact order and training trajectory (exploratory)}

Interleaving all context facts in one random order leaves the class unchanged at n=5, 6 and 8 (n=6: L 0.886, O 0.908, G 0.647). We also scored 6 of the 21 released training checkpoints (2 symbol draws). The checkpoints at 0 and 5k steps are R, and those from 10k on are non-R; the upstream training loss drops sharply between those steps. After 20k, Latin and loop accuracy plateau at 0.86--0.91, while g(G t0) keeps rising, from 0.49 at 10k to 0.65 at 100k. The class therefore changes during training.

\paragraph{Mechanism split (post hoc)}

The model partly answers by commutative copying. In non-abelian targets, when the transposed cell is revealed but differs from the queried cell, the model returns the transpose in 38\% (n=6) to 46\% (n=8) of cases. The appropriate baseline for G cells is a loop-level learner, which chooses uniformly among the values a loop completion of the cue allows, computed exactly. G cells are by definition not loop-forced, so beating this learner requires group structure beyond identity and cancellation. With the transpose hidden, the model beats it at n=6 (+0.148 [+0.130, +0.166]) and n=8 (+0.254 [+0.236, +0.273]), so part of its associativity-forced accuracy goes beyond identity and cancellation. At n=5 it does not (+0.004 [$-$0.043, +0.048]).

What remains untested is the compounding branch (N against N\_iso against A) on a real network. Testing it requires a model with more symbol tokens.
