\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{What the study establishes}

The first result is a measurement that can tell abstraction from exemplar reuse in context. Exact forcing classes and controlled histories (a length-matched scramble, held-out isomorphism types, a leak control and non-associative loops) give distinct, preregistered signatures for recall, Latin bookkeeping, exemplar matching, abstraction and Bayes-with-prior. The decision rule recovers all seven preregistered exact learners, plus the post-hoc count learner C, with no error (Section~\ref{sec:r-ideal}). Only held-out transfer cleanly separates abstraction from exemplar matching, and at prime $n$ the two are provably identical, so a claim of ``learning to learn'' an algebraic structure in context needs composite orders and held-out types.

The second is a calibrated null for pretrained language models up to 8B. None of the nine checkpoints (ten model--precision configurations) from three families infers in direct-answer mode, and none of the eight swept over cue density does so even at the densest cue, where row/column elimination would score 0.92 (a post-hoc baseline; Section~\ref{sec:r-cal}). All eight calibrated models are non-inferential on this format under the calibration rule with the $\geq 30$-query guard, and the two that qualify without it remain R in the preregistered $k = 16$ follow-up ($\mathrm{acc}_L$ 0.18 and 0.22). None compounds. Recall approaches ceiling for Qwen3 at 4--8B (0.95--0.96) but not for OLMo-2 (0.31--0.37) or SmolLM2 (0.44), so in Qwen3 the missing ingredient is the prerequisite inference, not reading the context.

The third is a shortcut that trained networks find instead of the task. A post-hoc diagnostic shows that small transformers trained from scratch on group, Latin and loop diets answer with the symbol least represented so far, a global count statistic that matches five of the six learned networks to within 0.001--0.007 (the 6-layer network exceeds it by 0.014) and accounts for the in-training plateau at $n = 6$: 0.33 for the shortcut, 0.29--0.36 for the networks (Section~\ref{sec:r-trained}). The fingerprint correctly gives the networks the class of the exact count learner (R), but the shortcut alone passes the preregistered learning-failure threshold (chance + 0.10). Future preregistrations should define ``learned'' against the count learner, not chance.

The fourth is a positive control on a real network. The released In-Context Algebra model~\cite{todd2026ica} is classified non-R, non-B: on the base $t = 0$ cells, Latin- and loop-forced cells score 0.89--0.99 and associativity-only cells 0.53--0.70, well above learner C and row/column elimination (Section~\ref{sec:r-ica}). Across six released checkpoints (exploratory), its class changes from R to non-R between 5k and 10k steps. The categorical classes miss its graded group prior (g(G t0) rises from 0.49 to 0.65 after the transition), which g(G t0) captures better as a continuous index than the B-type cut-off.

The fifth is a validity limit for activation-space ``mode'' probes. The compute--retrieve (CR) axis~\cite{ramdan2026cr} separates its calibration prompts with AUC 0.96--0.99, but it does not track retrieval versus inference once format and length are matched: it is significantly reversed in three of five models, and its sign flips with prompt format (Section~\ref{sec:r-cr}). An exploratory control attributes 64--87\% of the reversed gap to context vocabulary. With vocabulary matched, a retrieval signal of the predicted sign appears in the post-trained model (small, $d_z$ +0.36, comparable to its vocabulary effect) and without the chat template ($d_z$ +0.33 to +1.67). In base models under the chat template, the vocabulary effect is 4--12$\times$ the retrievability contrast.

\paragraph{What it does not establish}

We make no claim about larger models or test-time reasoning. The reasoning probe (Qwen3-1.7B, thinking on) was dominated by truncation: 28 of 30 thinking runs hit the 4,096-token budget, and the 2 that finished were correct (Section~\ref{sec:r-probe}). It neither shows nor excludes reasoning-enabled Latin inference, and it tests only whether a model can apply a \emph{stated} rule, not induce one from histories.

Validation on trained networks is only partial. The method-validation criterion of Experiment 3 is \emph{not met}: A4 and I4 are R, not A/B-type and N\_iso, and the preregistered depth claim is not supported. A post-hoc diagnostic attributes this to the training rather than to the fingerprint: the networks learned a count shortcut, and the fingerprint gives them the same class (R) as the exact count learner C. The In-Context Algebra model supplies a positive control for steps 1--3 of the rule, but its 16-token vocabulary rules out the compounding branch, so N versus N\_iso versus A on a real network remains untested.

Nor does Experiment 6 isolate which part of the training matters. The In-Context Algebra model has about 16$\times$ our parameters, but its checkpoints leave class R after about 0.64--1.28B training tokens, comparable to our roughly 0.91B, so the token budget does not explain the difference. Width (1024 vs 256), learning rate, symbol vocabulary (16 vs 64 symbols), loss target (every token vs answers) and context density (groups-only, 200-fact sequences vs sparse cues) also differ. Showing the A signature on a trained network needs a model of this kind with enough vocabulary for $t \geq 2$ histories, or a curriculum that defeats the count shortcut at small scale, such as a loss on cells where the least-revealed symbol is wrong.

The three largest models (Qwen3-4B-Base, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-8B-Base) ran in nf4 to fit the 8 GB GPU. The preregistered bf16-versus-nf4 control on Qwen3-1.7B-Base failed its tolerance: nf4 lowered G accuracy by 0.02--0.07 and changed 44\% of per-query answers. It created no spurious effect and preserved strong context use, but with nothing to hide at 1.7B it cannot rule out that nf4 hides a weak effect at 4B, 7B or 8B. nf4 accuracies should not be compared directly with bf16 levels.

The results are also tied to one format: unordered lines of single-token common English words used as arbitrary labels. In an exploratory row-sorted variant, sorting the target's facts helps at $k = 28$, about equally in Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base (+0.10 to +0.11) and less (+0.005 to +0.046) in every other model, including the larger OLMo-2-7B (+0.045). An exploratory instruction header does not help ($-$0.08 to +0.04, mean $-$0.006). Grids or natural-language framing may lower the onset scale. The fingerprint itself is format-independent, because the classes depend only on the cue.

\paragraph{Threats to validity and how each was handled}

Context length is controlled by a token-matched scramble history for every compounding contrast; two reliable raw $t = 0$ to $t = 4$ increases (OLMo-2-1B at $n = 6$, Qwen3-0.6B at $n = 8$) disappeared against it. Fresh single-token words per table, a random bijection and a semantic blacklist limit leakage through tokens. The audits recomputed the forcing classes of all 2,800 Experiment 1--2 stimulus trials with independent SAT and enumeration code (0 mismatches), as did the same checker on the 12,000 queries of the 600 later addendum-2d trials.

Batched, offloaded and version-mixed scoring were each checked against sequential scoring. Argmax agreement was 92--98\%, with near-ties in bf16; the Qwen3-1.7B-Base primary contrast, re-scored with one code version, gave $-$0.006 against $-$0.007; and classes are identical on accuracy and on $p_{\mathrm{gold}}$.

Freezing the rule and thresholds before any output limits analysis flexibility. Experiment 3's allowed adaptations (a 2$\times$-steps retrain of A4, an M=8 rerun of P4) did not trigger: A4 passed the learning rule, and P4 did not generalise. One change did matter. The $\geq 30$-query guard on the $k_L$ rule, added after the first sweep had been seen, excluded the $k = 16$ operating point that the frozen rule triggers for Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base (2 of 4 L queries correct at $k = 6$); run after the final audit, it leaves both R. Apart from the guard, no unplanned change (Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}) altered a stimulus, threshold or decision rule. Post-hoc analyses are labelled and enter no preregistered classification. Learner C, post hoc in Experiment 3, was fixed before Experiment 6 was preregistered and is its preregistered comparator (prediction P4 in Table~\ref{tab:app-ica-pred}).

Two adversarial audits (2026-10-07, 2026-10-09) re-derived every Experiment 1--5 number that existed at the time; later verification passes (2026-10-09 to 2026-10-11) re-derived the results produced after them (learner C, the count-shortcut diagnostic, the offload and re-scoring checks, the full Experiment 5b run and the addendum-2d run), checked the revised text, and checked Experiment 6 (2026-10-11). They corrected an inflated copy-bias statistic, an unguarded partial-file value, order-dependent bootstrap seeds, stale ranges and model counts, an unapplied learning-failure rule, an overstated ``dense-context Latin inference'' reading of the trained networks, and the post-hoc guard that had removed the preregistered $k = 16$ follow-up. None changed a fingerprint classification.

\paragraph{Implications}

For in-context learning research, ``the model improves after seeing related examples'' is weak evidence of abstraction unless:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item the improvement survives a length-matched control;
  \item the cells measured are forced only by the structure in question;
  \item the improvement transfers to held-out types.
\end{enumerate}

Likewise, ``the model solves more cells as the cue grows'' is weak evidence of constraint inference unless it beats a global count baseline. The released stimulus generator, exact forcing classes, idealised learners (now including C) and decision rule make these tests routine, and Experiment 6 shows that they are not blind: on a network trained for the task they return a non-R class and an associativity deficit, consistent with its published mechanisms~\cite{todd2026ica}.

For experience compounding more broadly, these results place the phenomenon, if it exists for algebraic abstractions, beyond the scale and inference mode tested here. They also give a concrete, falsifiable target: the onset of sparse-cue Latin inference above the count baseline should precede any compounding, and compounding with $w \approx 1$ should follow.

For representation-level claims about ``modes'' of processing, the CR result is a cautionary case: a direction that separates prompt \emph{types} need not track the \emph{process}. A format- and length-matched behavioural contrast, like leak versus base, is a cheap test that any such probe should pass before it is interpreted.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We asked whether a model that improves on a structured task after earlier examples in context has abstracted the structure or reused the examples, and we built a compounding fingerprint that answers this exactly for partial Cayley tables. Labelling each queried cell by its forcing class and controlling the history with a length-matched scramble, held-out types, a leak control and loops yields a preregistered decision rule that recovers seven exact idealised learners without error. Nine checkpoints (ten model--precision configurations) from three families, up to 8B, are recall-only and do not compound, although the larger Qwen3 models recall a seen table almost perfectly. Small transformers trained from scratch learn a global count shortcut, and the fingerprint assigns them the same class (R) as the exact count learner C. The released In-Context Algebra model is classified non-R, non-B: it infers Latin- and loop-forced cells almost perfectly but associativity-forced cells only in part. The compute--retrieve (CR) axis does not track retrieval versus inference once format and length are matched; in an exploratory control, context vocabulary accounts for most of its reversal.

Three problems remain open. First, the compounding branch of the rule, which separates N, N\_iso and A, is still untested on a real network. It needs a task-trained model with a symbol vocabulary large enough for histories of two or more tables, which the 16-token In-Context Algebra model cannot hold. Second, training for in-context algebra should be count-shortcut-aware: ``learned'' should be judged against learner C rather than chance, and a curriculum may need to penalise the shortcut directly. Third, activation probes for processing ``modes'' should pass matched-vocabulary contrasts before their projections are interpreted. Until then, a claim of in-context abstraction needs length-matched controls, structure-specific cells, held-out types and a count baseline.

\section*{Statements}

\paragraph{Preregistration}

Experiments 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 were preregistered in dated files frozen before the outputs they govern: 2026-10-06, 2026-10-07, 2026-10-07, 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-11. The exceptions are Experiment 5, whose file was finalised minutes after a discarded six-trial smoke test, and the $\geq 30$-query guard on the Experiment 2 $k_L$ rule, appended after the first calibration sweep had been seen (Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}, row 4). Experiment 4 and Experiment 5b were exploratory designs written down before their final runs: Experiment 4 was redesigned after its first run was truncated, and Experiment 5b followed a 20-trial audit pilot of the same design (Section~\ref{sec:probe}; Section~\ref{sec:cr}). Later notes were appended to these files, never edited in. Every deviation is listed in Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}.

\paragraph{Audits}

Two adversarial audits (2026-10-07 and 2026-10-09) re-derived every Experiment 1--5 number that existed at the time from the raw result files, using independent code. The results produced after the second audit (learner C, the count-shortcut diagnostic, the offload and re-scoring checks, the full Experiment 5b run and the addendum-2d run) were re-derived instead by later verification passes (2026-10-09), and further passes checked Experiment 6 and the assembled manuscript (2026-10-11). Each confirmed discrepancy was corrected, and the corrections that changed a reported number or verdict are listed in Section~\ref{sec:discussion} and Appendix~\ref{app:deviations}.

\paragraph{Compute}

All model inference and training used a single laptop GPU (NVIDIA RTX 5070, 8 GB). Exact learners, SAT computations and all analyses ran on the CPU.

\paragraph{Use of AI assistance}

Substantial AI assistance was used throughout this project. An AI system (Claude, Anthropic), working under the author's direction, contributed to the study design, wrote the code and the preregistrations, ran the experiments, analyses and audits, and drafted the text of this paper. The author takes responsibility for the content.

\paragraph{Competing interests}

The author also wrote the compute--retrieve preprint tested in Experiment 5~\cite{ramdan2026cr}. Experiment 5 was preregistered before scoring, its hypothesis and decision rule were fixed in advance, and its result, which does not support the preprint's detector on this contrast, is reported in full. The author declares no other competing interests.

\paragraph{Code and data availability}

Code, stimuli, results and preregistrations are available at \url{https://github.com/Somebodyhere101/compounding-fingerprint}. The repository contains the stimulus generator, the exact forcing-class labels, the idealised learners, the decision rule, all scoring and training scripts, every raw result file, the audit scripts and the preregistrations.

\section{Full results for the learners, models and networks}\label{app:main}

Table~\ref{tab:app-main-class} and Table~\ref{tab:app-main-g} give the complete main table: every idealised learner except Asl (which the rule classifies A at $n = 6$ and $n = 8$; Section~\ref{sec:r-ideal}), and every pretrained model and trained network, scored on the identical 1,800 trials. Classes come from the unchanged preregistered decision rule, applied both to accuracy and to mean $p_{\mathrm{gold}}$; the R threshold at $n = 6$ is $\mathrm{acc}_L < 0.417$, and chance on G cells is 0.167. Contrasts carry trial-bootstrap 95\% CIs (2,000 resamples, with seeds fixed per test so that the intervals are reproducible).

Three caveats apply to these tables. First, \textsuperscript{\dag} marks nf4: the preregistered quantisation control failed its tolerance (maximum per-cell G difference 0.067), so absolute G accuracy is biased low by about 0.04 and per-query predictions are unstable, although at 1.7B the class and the t4 $-$ scramble contrast are unchanged. Second, learner C was added post hoc (2026-10-09). Third, for the trained networks class R means only that $\mathrm{acc}_L$ is below threshold: every network also fails the leak control, so it neither recalls nor infers at sparse cues. P4 is \emph{not learned} under the Experiment-3 learning-failure rule and is excluded from method validation.

The preregistered derived quantities comp, held and $w$ are meaningful only above class R, because the rescaling g is undefined when $\mathrm{acc}_L$ is near chance. For the idealised learners at $n = 6$ they separate as designed: N\_iso has comp +0.819 [+0.772, +0.861] and held $-$0.002 [$-$0.043, +0.039] ($w \approx 0$), A has comp and held both +0.839 [+0.802, +0.856] ($w$ = 1.00), and N has comp $-$0.013 [$-$0.064, +0.023]. For every class-R model and network these quantities are uninterpretable, and we do not report them.

\section{Calibration and the addendum-2d operating point}\label{app:calib}

The cue sweep of Experiment 2a used $n = 6$, histories of $t = 0$ and $t = 4$ tables, and cues from $k = 6$ to $k = 28$ revealed cells, with 50 trials per combination of $t$ and $k$. \section{Trained networks: the count-shortcut diagnostic}\label{app:trained}

The diagnostic is post hoc. For each trial it defines the least-revealed set, the target words with the fewest occurrences as a result among the revealed cue facts, and it records three quantities: the within-trial constancy of the predictions, the share of predictions that fall in the least-revealed set, and the expected accuracy of learner C (uniform over that set) and of one-pass row/column elimination. At $n = 6$ the least-revealed set holds 0.28--0.34 of the target words, which is therefore the share expected from uniform guessing.

Table~\ref{tab:app-trained-count} summarises all raw-format cells for each run. The learned networks other than A6 put 85--99\% of their predictions in the least-revealed set and match learner C's accuracy to within 0.007; A4 matches it to within 0.001 on both the 1,800 main trials and the 500 cue-sweep trials. A6 is less constant (75\% in the set) and beats C by +0.0135. P4, which is \emph{not learned}, puts 28\% of its predictions in the set, about the uniform rate, and falls 0.048 below C. The two pretrained models we diagnosed do not follow the shortcut: Qwen3-8B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base put 31--42\% of their predictions in the set, and Qwen3-8B-Base exceeds C on the main trials only because those include its near-perfect leak-control cell (0.970).

The shortcut also accounts for the in-training plateau. Table~\ref{tab:app-trained-intrain} applies learner C and row/column elimination to the in-training evaluation conditions, teacher-forced and generated with the training generator. Over all remaining facts, the shortcut scores about 0.33 at $n = 6$ and 0.25 at $n = 8$, while elimination would score about 0.70 at $n = 6$. The networks reach 0.29--0.36 at step 14,000. On the identical sequences, averaged over the five evaluation conditions of each order, A4, G4 and I4 sit within $\pm 0.006$ of the shortcut at $n = 6$ and $n = 8$ (single conditions, 64 sequences each, within about $\pm 0.02$), A1 and A2 sit below it, and A6 sits slightly above it (+0.015 at $n = 6$). Their first-fact accuracy after the cue (0.23 for A4 and 0.21 for I4 at step 14,000; chance 0.17) is near the shortcut's level (0.20) and well below elimination (0.30).

Under the preregistered learning-failure rule, every run except P4 exceeds chance + 0.10 (0.267) on in-training $n = 6$ remaining-fact accuracy, with maxima of 0.33--0.36. P4 never does (maximum 0.183): it memorised its pool (training loss 0.005) without transfer to fresh symbols. Because the count shortcut alone scores 0.33, this threshold cannot distinguish learning the task from learning the shortcut. P4's in-training value on the isomorphic-copy condition (1.000) is an artefact of pool mode, in which the generator returns memorised pool tables, and it is not used anywhere.

\section{The compute--retrieve axis}\label{app:cr}

Table~\ref{tab:app-cr-h1} reports the preregistered H1 test of Experiment 5 for each model, together with the exploratory raw-format projection at the same layer. The detector layer is the best of four candidates by calibration AUC. In detector (chat-template) format, base $-$ leak is significantly negative in three models and null in two, so H1 (base $>$ leak, with the CI excluding 0 in at least 3 of 5 models) is supported in 0 of 5. In raw format, base $>$ leak with the CI excluding 0 in Qwen3-0.6B-Base, Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base, which would meet the criterion had raw format been primary, and base $<$ leak in Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B-Base. H2 (projection rising from L to O to G within base) is null in four models and significantly reversed in Qwen3-1.7B-Base ($\rho$ = $-$0.113 [$-$0.176, $-$0.046]); the other four $\rho$ lie between $-$0.065 and $-$0.003. In an exploratory analysis, projection does not predict correctness within a condition (AUC 0.46--0.55, except 0.38 in Qwen3-1.7B-Base leak).

Leak and base are matched in format, token count (281 context tokens in both) and query position, but not in vocabulary (Table~\ref{tab:app-cr-surface}). In leak, the history table is written in the target's own six words, so every target line, including the queried pair and its answer, appears verbatim; in base, the history uses six other words. In detector format the projected token is the template's newline after \texttt{assistant}, so the projection summarises the whole context.

Experiment 5b (exploratory, not preregistered) was written down before its full run but after a 20-trial audit pilot, so it is a full-sample estimate of an effect already seen, not an independent test. It changes only the history table. leakRel deranges the words of leak's history, which keeps its vocabulary but makes its answers inconsistent; baseRel writes base's history in the target's words, which keeps it non-retrievable. The share of the target's displayed lines found verbatim in the history is 1.00 for leak, 0.08 for leakRel, 0.11 for baseRel and 0.00 for base. $f_{\mathrm{vocab}} = (\mathrm{baseRel} - \mathrm{base})/(\mathrm{leak} - \mathrm{base})$ is the share of the base--leak gap reproduced by vocabulary alone, and leakRel $-$ leak is the cleanest retrievability contrast (predicted $> 0$). The control used uncached forwards, all 26 queries and 100 trials on four models (8B was not run), so its base $-$ leak values in Table~\ref{tab:app-cr-ctrl} differ slightly from Table~\ref{tab:app-cr-h1}.

In the three reversed base models under the chat template, vocabulary reproduces 64--87\% of the base--leak gap, the remainder (leak $-$ baseRel) is still reversed, and with vocabulary held fixed the retrievable context projects \emph{more} toward compute in Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base and no differently in Qwen3-4B-Base. The predicted direction appears in the post-trained model in both formats ($d_z$ +0.36 and +0.69) and in all four models in raw format at the detector layer ($d_z$ +0.33 to +1.67); at other layers the sign varies. In the post-trained model, vocabulary overlap raises the projection (baseRel $-$ base = +1.8) about as much as retrievability lowers it (leak $-$ leakRel = $-$1.3), which is why the preregistered contrast is null there.

\section{In-Context Algebra positive control}\label{app:ica}

We re-implemented the released model from its code without executing that code, and loaded the checkpoint with \texttt{weights\_only=True}. A second, independent forward pass (explicit causal attention, real-valued RoPE, erf-GELU) agrees with the adapter on 3,200 of 3,200 answer positions, with a maximum absolute logit difference of $1.9 \times 10^{-4}$. Table~\ref{tab:app-ica-valid} gives held-out final-fact accuracy on the model's own task. Under the upstream evaluation protocol on 1,024 fresh sequences, the released best checkpoint scores 0.959, below the 99.4\% that its authors report~\cite{todd2026ica}. Their figure is the maximum over up to about 290 training-time evaluations on one cached 512-sequence set, and \texttt{algebra\_gpt\_best.pt} was saved at that maximum; the 20k--100k checkpoints score 0.960--0.975 on our sequences. The shortfall is therefore consistent with snapshot selection on a fixed set, not with a port error. Full-sequence training loss is 0.917, against about 0.93 at the end of the upstream curve.

Two mechanisms are visible. When a non-abelian target's transpose is revealed but differs from the queried cell, the model copies it 38\% ($n = 6$) or 46\% ($n = 8$) of the time, a commutativity shortcut that fails on non-abelian groups. With the transpose hidden, the model beats the loop-level learner at $n = 6$ (+0.148 [+0.130, +0.166]; 282 trials, 2,819 cells) and at $n = 8$ (+0.254 [+0.236, +0.273]; 300 trials, 8,124 cells), but not at $n = 5$ (+0.004 [$-$0.043, +0.048]; 53 trials, 463 cells). At $n = 6$ and $n = 8$, then, part of its associativity-forced accuracy goes beyond identity and cancellation. Pooled by target type, G accuracy is 0.561 for S3 and 0.694 for Z6 at $n = 6$, and ranges from 0.475 (Q8) to 0.868 (Z2$\times$Z2$\times$Z2) at $n = 8$.

\section{Implementation and provenance details}\label{app:impl}

This appendix collects implementation checks and provenance details that the main text only summarises.

\paragraph{Scoring paths}

Each trial's prefix is encoded once. Queries with equal suffix length are scored in chunks of up to B on a copy of the prefix KV cache; from 2026-10-07 21:25 a one-query chunk is instead scored on the prefix cache itself, which is then cropped back (identical arithmetic).

B is set per trial from a KV-memory budget, and from 2026-10-07 13:16 it is halved after an out-of-memory error; it therefore varies with context length and hence with condition. For example, OLMo-2-7B used B = 8 at $t = 0$ and B = 1 at $t = 4$. From 2026-10-07 13:16 each scoring process was capped at 60\% of GPU memory (62\% for OLMo-2-7B).

On the Experiment-1 models, batched and sequential scoring agreed on 94--98\% of argmax decisions (max $|\Delta p_{\mathrm{gold}}|$ 0.05, near-ties). The four $n = 6$ cells that enter Qwen3-1.7B-Base's primary contrast were re-scored with the final code and B = 1. Per-cell G accuracy moved by at most 0.005, and t4 $-$ scramble was $-$0.006 [$-$0.034, +0.021] against $-$0.007 [$-$0.037, +0.020] originally (\texttt{exp2/\allowbreak{}offchk\_result.md}).

\paragraph{CPU-offload path for the 7--8B models}

For Qwen3-8B-Base and OLMo-2-7B, token embeddings were looked up on the CPU from the bf16 checkpoint weights, and the output projection was computed on the CPU in float32. We compared this path with standard scoring.

The 4B check is the configuration used for 8B.

\paragraph{CR-axis projections}

The cached forward path used for every Experiment-5 projection was checked in an audit against full uncached forwards. The two agreed with r $\geq$ 0.996 and a median relative difference $\leq$ 3.5\%, and sample condition differences were reproduced within 1.3 units.

In Experiment 5b, Qwen3-0.6B-Base ran one query per forward pass. The other three models ran the 26 queries of a trial-condition in one batched forward pass. Every row has the same token length, so no padding occurs, and a three-trial check reproduced the per-query projections exactly.

\paragraph{In-Context Algebra model}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Checkpoint:} \texttt{algebra\_gpt\_best.pt} from the authors' project page, sha256 9c0ee347\ldots{}a265d9.
  \item \textbf{Code:} read at commit 532a6a2, never executed. The model was re-implemented and loaded with \texttt{weights\_only=True}.
  \item \textbf{Independent check:} a second forward pass (explicit causal attention, real-valued RoPE, erf-GELU) agreed with the adapter on 3,200 of 3,200 answer positions (max $|$logit difference$|$ $1.9 \times 10^{-4}$).
  \item \textbf{Interpreter:} Windows Smart App Control blocked the GPU environment's virtual-environment launcher on 2026-10-11, so these runs used the base CPython 3.12 interpreter with the same installed packages (torch 2.7.1+cu128).
\end{itemize}

Two further notes apply. The resume path overwrites \texttt{config.json} with the arguments of the resume invocation; we checked these by hand against the original runs, and they match on every setting that affects the schedule and data. The learning-rate schedule is continuous across every resume, with every logged learning rate matching the planned schedule and no loss discontinuity, so the continuations in rows 10, 12 and 13 (row 11 is a from-scratch retrain with the same seed), although not among the preregistered allowed adaptations, only complete the preregistered schedule.
